name: Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil
native: עץ הדעת טוב ורע · etz ha-da'at tov va-ra
era: Second Temple period codified (6th c. BCE onward)
tree: Unspecified (interpreted as fig, grape, or wheat in later exegesis)
story: In the Garden of Eden, God plants a garden and sets in it two trees: the Tree of Life and the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. God commands Adam and Eve not to eat from the tree of knowledge, but the serpent tempts them. They eat, gain the knowledge of good and evil, and are cast from the garden, where cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way to the Tree of Life.
history: The narrative in Genesis 2-3 is among the oldest and most retold creation myths in world literature. Later Jewish, Christian, and Islamic exegesis debated the tree's identity — the Targums and Church Fathers proposed the fig (the fig-leaf in Eden), the vine, or wheat. Medieval and Renaissance art fixed the tree as a central image of original sin and redemption.
details: The tree functions as the archetypal forbidden fruit and the boundary between innocence and self-awareness. Its pairing with the Tree of Life encodes a theology of mortality: eating knowledge brings death, while the guarded Tree of Life offers the immortality humans forfeited. It became the single most reproduced 'tree of life' in Western art, from Byzantine icons to the Gothic Book of Kells and beyond.

name: The Lapis Tree of Gilgamesh
era: Sumerian period; Epic of Gilgamesh ca. 2100-1200 BCE
story: After killing Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest of the gods, the hero Gilgamesh and his companion Enkidu journey to the land of the gods. In some versions Gilgamesh receives a wondrous tree (a lapis tree or a 'tree of life' / 'plant of immortality') that confers eternal life; he leaves it behind, and it is lost to the mortal world.
history: The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest known great work of literature. The episode where Gilgamesh seeks the plant of immortality and it is snatched by a serpent is a direct narrative ancestor of the Eden story and of countless 'quest for the elixir' myths. Mesopotamian palace reliefs show stylized sacred trees (the 'tree of life' motif) with a deity at the base, a standard icon from the 4th millennium BCE onward.
details: The Mesopotamian sacred tree — often a cypress or cedar with banded trunk and a star or deity at its base — is one of humanity's oldest continuous visual symbols. It marks the axis between earth and heaven and the seat of divine kingship. The lost plant of Gilgamesh embodies the recurring theme of immortality glimpsed and then forfeited.

name: Sumerian Tree of Life (Nigal)
story: In Sumerian myth the sacred tree stands at the meeting of heaven and earth. The goddess Inanna (Ishtar) descends and ascends through the tree; the tree is the ladder of the cosmos. Kings offer libations to the tree, and it is depicted with the sun-disc and the eight-pointed star at its crown.
history: The 'tree of life' is a near-universal Mesopotamian motif, appearing on cylinder seals, reliefs, and temple architecture from the Early Dynastic period through the Neo-Assyrian era. It was a focus of royal and divine ritual, and its form — a tall trunk, tiered crown, and a star — became a fixed iconographic grammar.
details: The tree is the axis mundi: the point where the realms of gods and humans intersect. Its crown bears the sun (or star), its trunk is often banded like a column, and a deity or king appears at its base. This grammar of 'tree = cosmos' recurred for four millennia and influenced the sacred trees of every Near Eastern culture that followed.

name: Sycamore of the Goddesses (Ishked)
story: The sycamore tree is the living body of the goddesses Hathor and Isis. In the myth of Osiris, Isis shelters and resurrects her husband beneath the sycamore; the tree becomes a symbol of rebirth, the afterlife, and the nurturing of the dead. The goddess is depicted seated in, or emerging from, the tree, offering water and life to those who pass.
history: The sycamore is one of Egypt's most sacred trees, attested from the Old Kingdom. It appears in temple reliefs, on tomb walls of the Valley of the Kings, and in the Book of the Dead (Spell 113, 'The Tree of Isis'), where the deceased asks the ished tree for cool water and shade. The tree was planted in temple precincts and offered as a cult object.
details: The ished tree is a symbol of the afterlife's nourishment, of the goddess as mother, and of cyclical renewal. It links the living and the dead, offering shade, water, and breath — the essentials of life. Its iconography (goddess in a tree, offering cup) is a direct precursor to later 'goddess in the tree' and 'tree of paradise' motifs.

name: The Ba-Tree / Djed Pillar
story: The djed (or wedjety) pillar is a stylized tree-trunk — a cedar with bound horizontal bars — representing the spine of Osiris and the stability of the afterlife. To 'stabilize the djed' was to ensure the deceased's successful passage into eternity and the enduring strength of the pharaoh's reign.
history: The djed appears from the Old Kingdom, carved on tombs and in temple chapels, often placed beside the ankh and the was-scepter as one of Egypt's core life-symbols. It was a physical cult object — a wooden pillar decorated with bands — ritually 'strengthened' in festivals.
details: Though a pillar, the djed is a tree-symbol: the living trunk of Osiris, bound and standing. It encodes endurance, the backbone of the world, and the guarantee of eternal stability. Paired with the tree of Isis, it completes the Egyptian grammar of the sacred tree as life, death, and resurrection.

name: Ashoka Tree (Zoroastrian)
story: The Ashoka (or 'asoka', the 'tree without sorrow') is a radiant sacred tree associated with divine kingship and paradise. In later Iranian and Indian traditions it blooms with jewels and fragrance, and its shade is the reward of the righteous. Kings are crowned beneath it, and it marks the garden of the gods (paradaiza, the root of 'paradise').
history: The Ashoka tree is a pan-Iranian and Buddhist sacred motif. In Zoroastrian eschatology it is a tree of the final renovation (Shakadagha). Its name and image traveled with Achaemenid and Sasanian art, and the same tree reappears in Buddhist iconography (the tree under which the Buddha's mother conceived) — a rare case of one tree shared by two great traditions.
details: The Ashoka embodies the 'paradise tree': a garden, a crown, and a blessing. It is the visual and narrative ancestor of the 'tree of paradise' in both Zoroastrian and Christian-adjacent imagery. Its double identity (Iranian + Buddhist) makes it a key node in the cross-cultural genealogy of the tree of life.

name: Haoma Tree
tree: Haoma (possibly ephedra or a sacred shrub)
story: Haoma is the sacred, life-giving plant whose juice (haoma) is pressed and drunk in Zoroastrian ritual to grant wisdom, inspiration, and immortality. The god Haoma (and its Vedic counterpart Soma) is the divine source of vitality and of the prophet's revelation — the 'tree' that pours forth the nectar of the gods.
history: Haoma is central to the Gathas (the oldest Zoroastrian hymns) and is the Iranian counterpart of the Vedic Soma. Its ritual pressing and drinking is one of the oldest continuous liturgical acts in the Iranian world. The plant's identity is debated (ephedra, pomegranate, or a lost species), but its role as the divine tree of revelation and life is unambiguous.
details: As the 'tree of revelation,' Haoma/Soma links the tree of life to prophecy, inspiration, and divine intoxication — a theme echoed in the Christian Eucharist, in the Greek kykeon, and in the Norse mead of poetry. It is the tree that gives humans the gods' own vitality.

name: Yggdrasil
story: Yggdrasil, the immense ash, stands at the center of all things, its roots drinking from three sacred wells (Urd, Mimisbrunnr, Hvergelmir) and its branches spanning the nine worlds. The squirrel Ratatoskr carries insults between the eagle at the crown and the dragon Níðhöggr gnawing at the roots. The nornir dwell at the root, the world-serpent coils below, and the tree itself is the living axis of the cosmos.
history: Yggdrasil is the most famous world-tree of the Indo-European West, recorded in the Poetic Edda (Völuspá) and Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (13th c.). It synthesizes older Germanic sacred-ash cults, the megalithic 'world pillar,' and the cosmographic tree that appears across Finno-Ugric, Slavic, and Baltic traditions. Its iconography survived in runestones and medieval woodwork.
details: Yggdrasil is the paradigm axis mundi: a single organism connecting underworld, midworld, and heaven, with sacred animals at every level. It encodes the idea that the world is one living tree, that time (the norns, the dragon) gnaws at its base, and that even the cosmic tree faces a doom (Ragnarök) and renewal. It is the reference image for 'tree of life' in the modern imagination.

name: Oak of the Dagda (Aedh)
era: Iron Age; medieval manuscripts (12th c. CE)
story: The great god Dagda (the 'good god') is associated with the oak, the hazel of wisdom, and the cauldron of plenty. The oak is the tree of sovereignty, of the druids, and of the otherworld (Tír na nÓg). The hazel trees of wisdom drop nuts whose knowledge fills the Well of Segas; the oak shelters the druids' sacred groves and the seats of kings.
history: Celtic sacred trees (oak, ash, hazel) are central to the mythology of Ireland, Wales, and Britain. The oak (Quercus) is the tree of the druids, of strength, and of the otherworld. The 'world tree' and the sacred grove (nemeton) are attested in Iron Age and classical sources (Caesar, Diodorus) and persist in the medieval Irish and Welsh romances.
details: The Celtic grammar of the sacred tree is rich: oak = sovereignty and strength; hazel = wisdom; ash = the world pillar; apple = the otherworld. The tree is a portal to Tír na nÓg, a seat of kingship, and a font of druidic knowledge. It is the European 'tree of life' in its most mythologically dense form.

name: World Tree of Perun (Oak)
story: The Slavic world-tree (an oak, sacred to the storm-god Perun) stands at the center of the cosmos, its crown in the heavens of the gods, its trunk through the midworld, and its roots into the underworld (Nav). The tree is the axis connecting the three realms and the seat of divine thunder. The oak groves of the Slavs were centers of sacred law, oath, and sacrifice.
history: Christian chronicles (e.g., the Tale of Bylina, the 'Perun' oak of Kiev) record that the Slavs worshipped the oak and the sacred grove. The world-tree motif is shared across Finno-Ugric, Baltic, and Slavic traditions, and the oak-god (Perun / Juras) parallels Zeus and Thor. The tree survived in folk custom as the 'grove' and the sacred oak.
details: The Slavic world-tree is the Indo-European axis mundi in its eastern form: oak (thunder), three realms, and a divine center. It is the bridge between the Norse ash and the Iranian tree, and it anchors the whole 'tree of life' family in the Slavic and Baltic world.

name: Tree of the Hesperides (Golden Apples)
story: In the far west, beyond Oceanus, the Hesperides tend a tree (or grove) that bears golden apples of immortality. The tree was a wedding gift of Gaia to the goddess Hera, guarded by the serpent Ladon and later by Atlas. Herakles' eleventh labor is to fetch the golden apples — a quest for the fruit of eternal life.
history: The Hesperides and their golden-apple tree appear in Homer's Odyssey and Iliad and in Hesiod's Theogony. The motif of the guarded tree of immortality in the far west is a classic Indo-European 'quest' and a likely source (or parallel) to the Eden and Gilgamesh 'plant of life' stories. The golden apple became a standard symbol of paradise and immortality in Greek and Roman art.
details: The Hesperides' tree is the 'tree of immortality' in its purest Greek form: a guarded, western, golden tree whose fruit is eternal life. It is the archetype for every 'forbidden/guarded fruit of life' narrative and for the iconography of paradise (the golden apple, the serpent, the far west).

name: Olive Tree of Athena
story: Athena and Poseidon competed for the patronage of the great city. Poseidon struck the rock and a spring of salt water gushed forth; Athena planted the first olive tree, giving the city food, oil, wood, and shade. The city took her name (Athens) and the olive became its sacred tree — a symbol of peace, wisdom, and civilization.
history: The olive is the sacred tree of Attica and of Athena, attested from the Geometric period. The olive crown was awarded to victors at the Panathenaic Games and the Olympic Games. The olive branch is the ancient symbol of peace, and the 'olive of Athena' is one of the most enduring tree-symbols of Western culture.
details: The olive encodes the tree of life as civilization: food, light (oil), and peace. It is the 'domesticated' tree of life — the tree that sustains a city and a way of life. Its iconography (the branch, the crown, the grove) is a direct line to the modern symbols of peace and prosperity.

name: Oak of Dodona (Zeus)
story: At Dodona, the oldest Greek oracle, the wind spoke through the leaves of a great oak. Zeus's will was read in the rustling of the sacred grove; the priestess (the 'peepul' or the 'oak') interpreted the leaves' whispers. Two doves sent by Zeus chose the site, and the oak became the mouth of the storm-god.
history: Dodona was Greece's first and oldest oracle, predating Delphi, and its sacred oak is the 'speaking tree' of Greek religion. The oak-god Zeus and his wind-reading tree are the direct ancestors of the sacred groves of Apollo and of the entire Mediterranean oracle tradition. The 'tree that speaks' is one of the oldest forms of the tree of life.
details: The Dodona oak is the tree of prophecy: the leaves are the god's tongue. It anchors the 'sacred grove' as a site of divine speech and makes the tree a medium between the human and the divine — the tree of life as the voice of the cosmos.
